items.stem: Before coding a game, why is it helpful to write down the goal and the win/lose rules?

options.text: It gives a clear plan so you know what to build and when the game ends
options.rationale: Correct: clear rules guide the build and define winning and losing.

options.text: It makes the computer run faster
options.rationale: Planning helps you, not the computer's speed.
A goal is what makes it a game.
Planning rules does not change costumes.

items.explanation: Correct: clear rules guide the build and define winning and losing.
items.provenance: original Mastemy item drafted by an AI agent; no external question source

items.stem: Which TWO of these help make a game fair and fun to play? (Select TWO.)

options.rationale: Correct: a clear goal makes the game fair.
Correct: testing with players improves the game.

options.text: Hiding the score so nobody can see it
options.rationale: Players usually need to see progress; hiding it is not required for fairness.

options.text: Making the player move off the screen forever
options.rationale: Letting the player leave the screen is a bug, not a feature.

items.explanation: Correct: a clear goal makes the game fair.

items.stem: Your falling stars only fall once and never come back. What should you add?

options.text: Code to reset each star to the top (and keep spawning) so they fall again
options.rationale: Correct: objects must be reset or respawned to keep the game going.

options.text: Nothing; games only need one star
options.rationale: A game usually needs objects to keep appearing.
Size does not make stars respawn.
Sound does not reset the stars' position.

items.explanation: Correct: objects must be reset or respawned to keep the game going.
